newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan cult guru throws murder trial into confusion.
newsitem.headline: Japan cult guru throws murder trial into confusion.

text.p: The cult leader accused of masterminding last year's Tokyo subway gas attack threw his murder trial into confusion on Friday by first admitting responsibility in a courtroom outburst and then declaring his innocence.
After weeks of stony silence during his months-long trial, Shoko Asahara surprised the court with his outburst during cross examination of a top disciple at the Tokyo District Court.
Asahara is guru of Aum Shinri Kyo (Supreme Truth Sect), a doomsday cult that prosecutors say planned to bring down the Japanese government with its attacks.

Asahara, who said he had heard from his "Gods", also warned court-appointed defence lawyers they would die if they continued questioning the disciple, Yoshihiro Inoue, the guru's top lieutenant about the gassing.
"Yoshihiro Inoue was formerly my disciple. He is also a man of accomplishment. I would like to shoulder responsibility for all incidents. So please stop questioning him," Asahara said.
"I was instructed by God in my detention cell this morning," Asahara, whose real name is Chizuo Matsumoto, told the judge.
"Proceeding with the cross-examination would dispel the light in people's souls and lead to a path of darkness," Asahara, dressed in his usual blue shirt and trousers, said in a firm tone.
It was the first time Asahara had publicly admitted to the subway attack in March last year, which killed 11 and made some 6,000 ill.
The court went into recess after Asahara's outburst, reconvening 40 minutes later.
After consulting with his lawyers during the recess, Asahara, 41, stood up and this time declared his innocence.
"Although I am completely innocent, I don't want to torment the great soul of a man like Inoue," he said.
The prosecution had called Inoue as one of its witnesses in Asahara's six-month-long trial for murder in the subway attack.
Since his arrest, Inoue has spoken out against Asahara, saying he was under the influence of the guru who directly ordered the attack.

Asahara sat quietly and attentively while Inoue testified, but began wincing and twitching his body as the defence team inquired about Inoue's participation in the refining of sarin and other nerve gases.
He then mumbled that he was losing his energy and that he felt danger was coming. Judge Fumihiro Abe then accepted the defence request for a brief recess and ended the day's session.
Asahara, arrested in May 1995, has been indicted on 17 charges ranging from murder to illegal production of drugs and weapons. He faces the death penalty by hanging if convicted.
He has refused to enter pleas in all of his trials.
But scores of his followers have testified in court in their own trials that he ordered the gas attacks and other crimes.

About 30 of Asahara's top lieutenants have also been indicted for the subway gassing, the murder of a follower who tried to quit the group, use of illegal drugs and attempts to mass-produce Russian-designed automatic weapons.

As well as being charged with the Tokyo subway attack, Asahara has been accused of masterminding a nerve gas attack on the central Japanese city of Matsumoto in July 1994 that killed seven people and made 600 ill.
The 10,000-member Aum Shinri Kyo, which has already been declared bankrupt, is under threat of extinction as Japan is expected to outlaw the doomsday cult in several months.
